screens.title: Functions, Visibility, and Modifiers
screens.subtitle: How Solidity functions are declared, protected, and optimized

narration.text: In this chapter we will learn how Solidity functions are written, how to control who can call them, and how to enforce preconditions safely. You will see the building blocks of a function declaration: parameters, return types, visibility, mutability, and optional modifiers. We will compare public, private, internal and external visibility and explain why choosing the right one is essential to prevent accidental exposure of internal logic. You will also learn when to mark a function view or pure to signal no state changes, saving unnecessary gas for off-chain calls. Modifiers let you reuse checks like onlyOwner so you don’t duplicate access control logic. Finally, we’ll cover the error primitives require, revert, and assert, and when to use each. Throughout, real code examples will show these concepts in action, and a hands-on RestrictedWallet exercise will let you practice. By the end you should be able to declare safe functions, reduce gas for read-only calls, and apply modifiers and error checks to protect critical operations.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Functions are the executable units in Solidity; visibility, mutability, modifiers, and error handling together define how they behave securely and efficiently.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives map to concrete developer skills. First, you will be able to define and implement functions with parameters and return values in Solidity, which means writing clear signatures, assigning explicit return variables when helpful, and calling functions both internally and externally. Second, you will master visibility specifiers by choosing public, private, internal, or external appropriately to control access to functions and state variables; this prevents accidental exposure and reduces attack surface. Third, you will learn to differentiate view and pure functions and apply them for gas optimization: marking read-only or computation-only functions correctly signals to the compiler and lets off-chain calls avoid transactions. Fourth, you will develop and apply function modifiers to enforce access control and preconditions, using the underscore placeholder to insert function bodies safely. Each objective is paired with a milestone so you can verify competency by implementing an example contract and tests that exercise the visibility and modifier behavior.

screens.title: What is a Solidity function?
screens.subtitle: Function anatomy: name, parameters, visibility, mutability, modifiers, returns

narration.text: A function in Solidity is an executable unit that encapsulates a specific action, whether changing state, computing a value, or calling another contract. The declaration includes the function name, typed parameters, visibility specifiers, optional state mutability like view or pure, optional modifiers which attach checks or behaviour, and a return type list. Naming return variables can make the body clearer and helps with readability. For example, a transfer function might be declared with an address parameter and a uint amount, and return a bool success flag. Parameters have explicit types and, when needed for reference types, a data location such as calldata. Think of a function signature as the public contract between caller and callee: it documents accepted inputs, promises about state access, and the expected outputs. A common misconception is that leaving visibility unspecified is harmless; in Solidity you must specify visibility for functions and variables because the compiler needs to enforce access rules. Another important point is the difference between internal and external calls: how arguments are passed and gas implications differ. As a takeaway, always write explicit signatures, pick the narrowest visibility that still supports required calls, and mark functions view or pure when they truly do not change state. How might that practice reduce both risk and cost in your contracts?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A function is a typed, declared unit of executable logic; its signature defines inputs, outputs, visibility, mutability, and attached behavior.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › What is a Solidity function?
Function anatomy
  • Name and typed parameters; reference types need locations like calldata.
  • Visibility controls who can call the function and how it’s exposed.
  • Mutability (view/pure) signals state access and impacts off-chain gas costs.
  • Modifiers insert reusable checks or behaviour at the call site.
Concrete example
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

function transfer(address recipient, uint amount) public returns (bool success) {
  // body: perform balance checks and transfer
  success = true;
}
Common misconception
Some developers assume unspecified visibility is inferred. Solidity requires explicit visibility. Failing to pick the appropriate visibility can expose helper functions to external calls or block derived-contract access incorrectly.
Key takeaway
Always declare full signatures and prefer the least permissive visibility that still supports required interactions; annotate view and pure when applicable to make intent and gas behavior explicit.

screens.title: Visibility Specifiers
screens.subtitle: public, private, internal, external — who can call what?

narration.text: Visibility specifiers define the access surface of functions and state variables and are a primary security control. Public is the most permissive: a public function can be called from outside the contract and also from within the contract itself. Public state variables automatically get a generated getter. Private is the most restrictive: private functions and variables are only accessible within the contract that defines them and are not visible to inheriting contracts. Internal sits in between private and public: internal members are accessible to the defining contract and any derived contracts but are not callable externally. External functions can only be invoked from outside the contract; they cannot be called internally, and they accept their parameters more efficiently via calldata which can save gas for external-only interfaces. A practical rule is to restrict helper functions to private or internal, expose only necessary APIs as external or public, and protect exposed functions with modifiers where appropriate. A common error is making sensitive state-mutating functions public without any access checks; this often leads to vulnerabilities. As a quick contrast: choose internal when derived contracts need to extend logic; choose private when you want an implementation detail hidden even from children. Which visibility would you pick for a reusable helper that must be overridden by derived contracts?

keyIdea.title: Visibility control
keyIdea.text: Use the narrowest visibility that fulfills the required calling pattern to reduce exposure and potential misuse.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Visibility Specifiers
Quick reference
  • public: callable externally and internally; public variables get a getter.
  • external: callable only from outside; gas-efficient for calldata parameters.
  • internal: usable inside contract and by derived contracts.
  • private: only inside defining contract; not visible to children.
Callability matrix
External caller
public, external
Internal call
public, internal, private (private only in defining contract)
Gas note
External functions use calldata which avoids copying into memory for certain types and can be more gas-efficient for API endpoints intended only for external callers.
Example scenarios
  • A helper function used only inside the contract: make it private.
  • Logic that derived contracts must call: make it internal so children can access it.
  • External API intended only for users: make it external and optimized for calldata parameters.
Key takeaway
Pick the tightest visibility compatible with required interactions. This reduces accidental exposure and simplifies audits.

screens.title: State Mutability: view vs pure
screens.subtitle: When to mark functions as read-only or computation-only

narration.text: State mutability specifiers communicate how a function interacts with contract state. A view function promises not to modify state: it may read state variables but will not change them. External callers can execute view functions off-chain at no gas cost because they do not create a transaction. If a view function is called internally by a state-changing function, however, it contributes to gas cost as part of that transaction. Pure functions are stricter: they promise neither to read nor modify state and operate only on input parameters and local variables. Pure functions are ideal for deterministic computations like arithmetic or string manipulation that do not depend on contract storage. Correctly labelling views and pure functions improves clarity for users and tooling, and enables free off-chain inspection. A misconception is to mark functions view simply because they appear harmless; ensure they truly perform no state writes, even indirectly. As an example, a getBalance function that returns balance should be view, while a calculateSum utility that only returns a + b should be pure. Marking functions accurately is both a developer signal and a gas optimization for users who call functions off-chain.

keyIdea.title: Mutability
keyIdea.text: Use view for read-only access and pure for computation-only functions to communicate intent and enable gas-free external calls.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › State Mutability
view
Reads state but does not modify it. Off-chain calls are gas-free. Be careful: internal use within a transaction still costs gas.
pure
Does not read or modify state. Ideal for deterministic calculations that depend only on inputs.
Examples
function getBalance() public view returns (uint currentBalance) {
  currentBalance = balance;
}

function calculateSum(uint a, uint b) public pure returns (uint) {
  return a + b;
}
Key takeaway
Label functions precisely: view for read-only access to storage, pure when no storage is involved. This helps users and optimizes gas for off-chain calls.

screens.title: Function Modifiers and the underscore placeholder
screens.subtitle: Create reusable guards like onlyOwner and where function bodies run

narration.text: Modifiers allow you to write reusable checks or behavior that execute before and/or after a function’s body. You declare a modifier with conditions and place an underscore token to indicate where the original function code will run. The typical onlyOwner pattern checks that msg. sender equals owner, calls require to revert if not, then continues to the function body. Modifiers can also apply multiple checks, and their order matters: the leftmost modifier is evaluated first. A subtle point is that modifiers can affect gas consumption: conditions run even when the function reverts, and any expensive checks add cost. A common misuse is embedding complex logic in modifiers that’s hard to reason about or that changes state in surprising ways. Use modifiers for clear, simple preconditions like authorization, and put heavier logic in internal helper functions. As a concrete example, an onlyOwner modifier calls require(msg. sender == owner, "Only the contract owner can call this function."); then contains underscore to proceed. When testing, ensure protected functions revert for non-owners and succeed for the owner. Finally, prefer explicit checks in code where readability would suffer from overusing modifiers.

keyIdea.title: Modifier pattern
keyIdea.text: Modifiers encapsulate reusable preconditions; the underscore token marks where the decorated function body executes.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Function Modifiers
Modifier pattern explained
  • Modifiers run code and use _; to insert the function body.
  • Use require inside modifiers to revert when preconditions fail.
  • Order of modifiers matters when multiple modifiers are applied.
Code example
modifier onlyOwner() {
  require(msg.sender == owner, "Only the contract owner can call this function.");
  _;
}

function setValue(uint newValue) public onlyOwner {
  _value = newValue;
}
Common mistake
Putting heavy state changes inside a modifier can hide side effects. Prefer pure checks in modifiers and move complex logic into internal functions called explicitly for clarity.
Key takeaway
Use modifiers for concise, standard preconditions like authorization. Keep them simple and readable so behavior is obvious during review and audit.

screens.title: AccessControl contract explained
screens.subtitle: A live walkthrough of state, functions, modifiers and mutability

narration.text: Let's walk through the provided AccessControl example to see how the pieces fit together. The contract sets owner as a public state variable in the constructor and maintains a private _value that represents internal state. The modifier onlyOwner checks msg. sender and reverts via require if the caller is not the owner; it places _; where the function body executes. Public functions like setValue are callable externally and internally and use onlyOwner to protect state changes. getValueExternal is declared external view: external prevents internal calls and view promises not to modify state. Internal and private helper functions show different visibility: an internal function _incrementValue is accessible within the contract and by derived contracts while a private function _decrementValue is accessible only within this contract. The calculateSum example is pure because it neither reads nor writes state. A misconception to avoid is assuming private equals secure in an inheritance context; private hides members from children. When reading this code, test both external and internal call paths and ensure modifiers cover sensitive state updates. What tests would you write to confirm onlyOwner behaves correctly and that external functions cannot be called internally?

keyIdea.title: Walkthrough
keyIdea.text: AccessControl demonstrates owner state, private/internal helpers, external/view functions, modifiers, and a pure utility function.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › AccessControl Walkthrough
AccessControl (selected snippets)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract AccessControl {
  address public owner;
  uint private _value;

  modifier onlyOwner() {
    require(msg.sender == owner, "Only the contract owner can call this function.");
    _;
  }

  constructor() {
    owner = msg.sender;
    _value = 0;
  }

  function setValue(uint newValue) public onlyOwner {
    _value = newValue;
  }

  function getValueExternal() external view returns (uint) {
    return _value;
  }

  function calculateSum(uint a, uint b) public pure returns (uint) {
    return a + b;
  }
}
Testing checklist
  • Call setValue from non-owner and expect revert with the modifier message.
  • Call getValueExternal from an external address — it should return the value and be gas-free off-chain.
  • Check that calculateSum returns deterministic results and does not access storage.
Concept callouts
owner is public; _value is private; onlyOwner manages access; view and pure show mutability intent.
Key takeaway
Reading example contracts shows how visibility, mutability, modifiers, and error checks combine to express both behavior and security intent.

screens.title: Error Handling: require, revert, assert
screens.subtitle: Choosing the right primitive for validation and invariants

narration.text: Error handling in Solidity is essential for safe contracts and good UX. Use require(condition, message) for validating inputs and preconditions that you expect may fail, such as checking that amounts are positive or balances are sufficient. When require fails, it reverts changes and returns the provided message, refunding unused gas. revert(message) is equivalent in effect but is often used deeper in complex logic or when you want to bail out with a clear message without a single conditional at the top. assert(condition) is intended for internal invariants that should never fail; if an assert triggers, it consumes remaining gas and signals a bug rather than a routine user error. Prefer require and revert for expected, user-facing checks, and reserve assert for invariants that indicate a deeper contract logic failure. A common misconception is overusing assert for input validation; that can unintentionally burn gas and confuse users. When designing functions like withdraw, check preconditions with require before performing state changes and external transfers. That pattern prevents inconsistent state and surfaces helpful error messages to callers and testing frameworks. Error Handling: require, revert, assert means use require for expected input checks, revert for complex bailouts, and assert only for invariants that indicate internal bugs.. In practical terms, choosing the right primitive for validation and invariants. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Error handling
keyIdea.text: Use require for expected input checks, revert for complex bailouts, and assert only for invariants that indicate internal bugs.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Error Handling
require
For validating inputs and preconditions. Returns a message and refunds unused gas on failure.
Example: require(balances[msg.sender] >= amount, "Insufficient balance.");
revert
Explicitly revert with a message when deeper logic detection requires bailout.
Example: if (someComplexCheckFails) { revert("Complex failure"); }
assert
Use only for invariants that indicate a bug. assert consumes remaining gas on failure.
Example: assert(totalSupply == sumOfBalances);
Best practices
  • Check inputs early with require to avoid wasted work.
  • Use revert for clear bailout paths deep in logic.
  • Reserve assert for invariants and internal consistency.
Key Takeaway

Prefer require and revert for expected error conditions to refund gas and give clear messages; use assert only for invariants that indicate a serious bug.

screens.title: Design pattern: Protecting state-changing functions
screens.subtitle: Use modifiers and require checks to enforce safe state transitions

narration.text: When you design state-changing functions, follow a simple defensive process: first validate inputs with require, next enforce authorization with a modifier like onlyOwner, then perform state updates, and finally execute external transfers or calls. Validating upfront avoids wasted computation and side effects. Using modifiers standardizes authorization logic so every protected function uses the same check and message. For example, a withdraw function should require that the amount is greater than zero and that the contract has sufficient balance. The onlyOwner modifier should then ensure the caller is authorized. After state updates, signal success or transfer funds. A common pitfall is performing an external call before updating internal balances, which can open reentrancy vulnerabilities. To avoid that, update state first, then call external addresses. Another misconception is thinking modifiers alone are enough; they must be paired with explicit precondition checks for inputs. As a checklist: validate inputs, enforce authorization, update contract state, then perform external actions. This ordering reduces common classes of bugs and makes auditing straightforward. Design pattern: Protecting state-changing functions means validate inputs, check authorization, update internal state, then perform external calls to minimize attack surface and reentrancy risk.. In practical terms, use modifiers and require checks to enforce safe state transitions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Safe ordering
keyIdea.text: Validate inputs, check authorization, update internal state, then perform external calls to minimize attack surface and reentrancy risk.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Protecting State
Defensive sequence
  1. Validate inputs with require to avoid invalid operations.
  2. Enforce authorization with a modifier like onlyOwner.
  3. Update internal state so balances reflect pending changes.
  4. Perform external calls or transfers after state is consistent.
Common mistake
Sending Ether to an external address before updating balances can enable reentrancy. Always update state first, then transfer.
Concrete withdraw example
Withdraw should require amount > 0, require contract balance >= amount, run onlyOwner, subtract amount from state, then transfer to owner using payable(owner).transfer(amount).
Key takeaway
Follow a predictable sequence of checks and updates to avoid logic errors and security vulnerabilities like reentrancy.

screens.title: RestrictedWallet: starter code and tasks
screens.subtitle: Implement owner, deposit, withdraw, getBalance, and onlyOwner modifier

narration.text: The RestrictedWallet activity lets you practice visibility, modifiers, mutability and error checking. The starter contract sets owner in the constructor. Your tasks are: define an onlyOwner modifier that requires msg. sender == owner, implement a public payable deposit function to receive Ether, implement a withdraw function protected by onlyOwner that uses require to check that the withdraw amount is positive and that the contract has sufficient balance, and add a public view getBalance function that returns address(this). balance. When coding, remember that deposit must be payable to accept Ether. For withdraw, after validating with require, perform the transfer using payable(owner). transfer(_amount). Test from different accounts: deposit from a non-owner account should succeed; withdraw from a non-owner should revert due to onlyOwner; withdraw with insufficient contract balance should revert due to require. This hands-on exercise verifies that visibility, modifiers and error handling actually behave as intended and gives you concrete scenarios to test. After implementing, try calling getBalance off-chain to observe its gas-free behavior. In practical terms, implement owner, deposit, withdraw, getbalance, and onlyowner modifier. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Starter code

pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract RestrictedWallet {
    address public owner;

    // Define onlyOwner modifier here

    constructor() {
        owner = msg.sender;

  • Make deposit payable so anyone can send Ether to the contract.
  • Protect withdraw with onlyOwner and require checks for amount and balance.
  • Return contract balance with a public view getBalance function.
  • Test deposit from non-owner, withdraw from non-owner, withdraw > balance, and getBalance off-chain.
Pro tip
Use clear revert messages in require so tests and users can diagnose failures quickly.

screens.title: Visibility and inheritance
screens.subtitle: How internal and private behave with derived contracts

narration.text: Inheritance changes what visibility means. Internal members are visible to derived contracts, which makes internal suitable for base contract logic that descendants extend or call. Private members are hidden from derived contracts; they exist only in the defining contract. This distinction matters when building base contracts intended for extension: mark functions internal if children must reuse or override them. A frequent mistake is using private for a helper that you later need in a child contract; that forces duplicate code or risky interface exposure. Another important aspect is that public state variables generate getters in the defining contract; derived contracts can read the state variable directly if it is declared internal or public, but not if it is private. When designing libraries or base contracts, document intended extension points and pick internal for overridable hooks. Also test inherited behavior by creating a derived contract that calls internal functions and verifying that private ones are inaccessible. This practice surfaces visibility assumptions early so you avoid architecture-level mistakes in larger systems. Visibility and inheritance means internal is visible to derived contracts, private is not; choose internal for extensible base behavior and private for strict encapsulation.. In practical terms, how internal and private behave with derived contracts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Inheritance visibility
keyIdea.text: internal is visible to derived contracts, private is not; choose internal for extensible base behavior and private for strict encapsulation.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Visibility & Inheritance
When to use internal
Use internal for helpers and hooks intended for derived contracts; they are accessible to children and allow reuse without exposing methods externally.
When to use private
Use private to strictly encapsulate implementation details that should never be visible or callable by children.
Architecture check
Design base contracts with explicit extension points. Document which functions are internal hooks and which are private helpers. This prevents surprises when building derived contracts or libraries on top of your base code.
Key takeaway
Choose internal for extensibility and private for strict encapsulation. Test derived contracts to confirm access expectations.

screens.title: Public vs External: performance and call semantics
screens.subtitle: When external is preferable and why calldata matters

narration.text: Public and external can appear similar but differ in call semantics and gas characteristics. A public function can be called both internally and externally. An external function is callable only from outside the contract. The key difference is how arguments are handled: external functions accept parameters via calldata, which avoids copying data into memory for certain reference types and can therefore be more gas-efficient for large arrays or strings passed only from external callers. If you know a function will only be invoked from off-chain wallets or other contracts, external is often the better choice. However, if you need to call the function from within the same contract or from derived contracts, public is necessary. A common misconception is switching to external everywhere for gas savings without considering internal usage — this leads to compilation errors or unexpected behavior. When optimizing, measure gas in a profiler or the Remix debugger to confirm benefits. The practical rule: prefer external for A P I endpoints intended only for external callers, use public when internal calls are needed, and test both call paths when in doubt.

keyIdea.title: Public vs External
keyIdea.text: External uses calldata and can be more gas-efficient for external-only APIs; public supports internal calls so choose based on intended usage pattern.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Public vs External
Public
Callable internally and externally. Use when you need to invoke from inside the contract.
Use case: utility functions called both from APIs and internal logic.
External
Callable only from outside. Parameters arrive in calldata, avoiding copies to memory for certain types and saving gas.
Use case: API endpoints receiving large arrays or strings from external callers.
Practical advice
When optimizing for gas, prefer external for functions designed solely for external invocation. If internal calls are needed, use public. Always measure the actual gas impact in a profiler.

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential ideas you should carry forward. First, functions are typed and declared units: always specify parameters, return types, visibility, mutability, and any modifiers so intent is explicit. Second, visibility controls access: public and external expose functions externally with different call semantics, internal is for inheritance points, and private hides implementation details from children. Choosing narrow visibility reduces attack surface. Third, use view and pure to signal read-only or computation-only behavior and to enable gas-free off-chain calls; use modifiers like onlyOwner to centralize authorization checks, and prefer require or revert for expected user-facing errors while reserving assert for invariants. These three rules—explicit signatures, least-permissive visibility, and clear mutability and error handling—form a robust foundation for writing secure, efficient Solidity functions. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Explicit declarations, minimal exposure, and clear mutability and error handling make functions safer and cheaper to use.

Two, visibility matters: internal for inheritance, private for strict encapsulation, external for external-only APIs, and public when both internal and external calls are needed. Three, use view and pure to mark read-only or computation-only functions and use require and revert for expected errors while reserving assert for internal invariants. Keep these short rules in mind as you implement the RestrictedWallet and other contracts, and always run simple tests that exercise both allowed and forbidden call paths to confirm visibility and modifiers behave as expected. Be explicit
